1.pericope_label: But it came to pass, that when Sanballat heard that we builded the wall, he was wroth, and took great indignation, and mocked the Jews. And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned? Now Tobiah the Ammonite was by him, and he said, Even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall. Hear, O our God; for we are despised: and turn their reproach upon their own head, and give them for a prey in the land of captivity: And cover not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before thee: for they have provoked thee to anger before the builders. So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the opening notice as characteristic of the book, a general statement made first and expanded afterwards, so that the mockery itself comes later; the brethren before whom Sanballat spoke are his counsellors and body-guard. He would render the second taunt not will they fortify themselves but will they leave them to themselves, taking the neighbouring nations as the subject while granting that contempt is not scrupulous or precise, and he identifies the question about sacrificing as the provocation of God that the prayer complains of. On the prayer he notes that it is Nehemiah's habit to turn everything to devotion as he goes, and that this one is full of an angry jealousy for the honour of a jealous God, whose tone of holy revenge pervades the Old Testament and has not altogether departed in the New. Delitzsch places the taunt publicly before the rulers of Samaria and its army, observes that the word for withered or powerless occurs here only, and rules out the older reading of the second question on the ground that all four must share one subject. He keeps the prayer to its sense, that Nehemiah asked God to turn the reproach upon the enemies' own head and give them for plunder in a land where they would dwell as captives, and not to cover, that is forgive, their iniquity, since they had openly challenged the divine wrath by despising him within the builders' hearing; and he reads the closing notice as meaning that no breach was left anywhere in the circuit up to half the wall's height.

Gill identifies the brethren Sanballat addressed as Tobiah and Geshem, and perhaps other governors of the Persian king in those parts, and notes that Nehemiah sent no answer to the men who had held him and his builders in contempt but applied to God instead. On the hardest clause he is careful: the petition that their sin be not blotted out is spoken not from a private spirit of revenge but from a public spirit for the glory of God and his justice, and not as a mere imprecation but as a prophecy of what would be the case, in the manner of many of David's petitions in the Psalms, with a foundation already laid in the threatened destruction of Moab and Ammon. Of the progress he says only that they went on building notwithstanding the scoffs and the threats.

Clarke observes that Sanballat, as governor, had command of the army and wished to excite the soldiers against the work, and generalises the tactics on display: the enemies of God's work despise the workmen, turn all into ridicule, have recourse to lying, and sometimes use fair but deceitful speeches. He says plainly that a prayer of this kind, understood literally, is not lawful for any Christian, being excusable only in a Jew under severe irritation, but holds that the clauses are probably declaratory rather than precative, since the same Hebrew form serves for both, and that they had respect only to the body and this life, amounting to no more than that what a man soweth he shall reap. On the last verse he finds the original emphatic, that the people had a heart to work, and adds that where the heart is engaged the work of God goes on well, noting also that the whole verse is omitted by the Greek. Wesley glosses the taunt about a day as asking whether they mean to begin and finish in one day, and the burnt stones as those broken by the Chaldeans when they took the city; on the imprecation he asks for judgments that would either reform the enemies or warn others by their example, explaining that God is said to cover sin when he forbears to punish it, and that the enemies had provoked not the builders only but God.

Henry takes the enemies' response in two parts, heart and word. In heart they were out of all patience, having pleased themselves that while Jerusalem lay unwalled they could swallow it up at will, for the strength and safety of the church are the grief and vexation of its enemies. In word they despised the work, which displayed their malice and yet served the builders, since by reckoning it a foolish undertaking that would sink under its own weight they did not try to obstruct it until too late; Sanballat scorned the workmen and Tobiah the work itself, profane scoffers sharpening one another. He marks that Nehemiah did not answer these fools according to their folly nor upbraid them with their weakness but looked up to God, and that God's people have often been a despised people, God hearing all the slights put upon them, which is their comfort and a reason they should be as though they were deaf. The imprecation he reads as spoken by a spirit of prophecy rather than of prayer, not to be imitated by those taught of Christ, and notes that its reason is not that the enemies abused us but that they provoked thee. He ends with two rules, that good work goes on well when people have a mind to it, and that the reproaches of enemies should quicken us to duty rather than drive us from it.

debates: Whether Nehemiah's imprecation may be prayed, where Clarke says that understood literally it is not lawful for any Christian and reads the verbs as declaratory, Henry calls it a spirit of prophecy rather than of prayer and not to be imitated, Gill denies any private revenge and makes it a prophecy from a public spirit, and Wesley keeps it as a petition for judgments that would reform the enemies or warn others.

What the second taunt asks, where Ellicott renders it will they leave them to themselves, taking the neighbouring nations as its subject, while Delitzsch rules that reading inadmissible because all four questions must share the same subject.

What the closing notice claims for the work, which Delitzsch takes to mean that no breach was left anywhere in the circuit up to half the wall's height, and Ellicott as the wall being now continuous to half its height.
outliers: Clarke notes that the whole verse recording the people's heart to work is omitted by the Greek.
Ellicott identifies the mockers' question about sacrificing as the very provocation of God that Nehemiah's prayer complains of.

7.pericope_label: But it came to pass, that when Sanballat, and Tobiah, and the Arabians, and the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites, heard that the walls of Jerusalem were made up, and that the breaches began to be stopped, then they were very wroth, And conspired all of them together to come and to fight against Jerusalem, and to hinder it. Nevertheless we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night, because of them. And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall. And our adversaries said, They shall not know, neither see, till we come in the midst among them, and slay them, and cause the work to cease. And it came to pass, that when the Jews which dwelt by them came, they said unto us ten times, From all places whence ye shall return unto us they will be upon you. Therefore set I in the lower places behind the wall, and on the higher places, I even set the people after their families with their swords, their spears, and their bows. And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses. And it came to pass, when our enemies heard that it was known unto us, and God had brought their counsel to nought, that we returned all of us to the wall, every one unto his work.

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the scale of the conspiracy small: the tribes enumerated were only small parties under the immediate influence of Sanballat, since nothing beyond that would have been likely among fellow subjects of Persia, and though they did not fear the Persian authority enough to refrain from resolving on an attack, they soon abandoned the project; the phrase rendered to hinder it he would translate rather to do it hurt. He would render the ground of the watch not because of them but over against them, opposite each point of their encampment, and notes that the setting of the watch was accompanied by solemn and united prayer. Of the complaint he observes that the writer gives a summary of difficulties, Judah complaining of a growing feebleness, especially as so many were diverted to the watches, and of the enemies' plan that it was evidently to watch and surprise rather than to make the threatened attack. On the posting he explains that the lower places were really the bare places, where the wall was not yet at its due height and approaching foes could be seen at a distance, and he judges that the appeal beginning with Nehemiah's looking was uttered on the actual approach of an attacking party. Delitzsch records the measures plainly, that Nehemiah and the superintendents of the work prayed and set a watch day and night to ward off a probable attack, that the watch added to continuous labour must have pressed heavily on the people, and that the neighbouring Jews came and said it again and again, since adversaries surrounded the community on every side.

Gill is brief here, but takes the key verb in its plain sense: when Nehemiah says that he looked, he took a view of the people, observing that they were in their proper place and sufficiently armed, and also whether the enemy was coming. He notes as well that the Jews who brought the warning dwelt near Samaria, Arabia and Ashdod and so came by their intelligence of the enemies' designs, that the lower places where the guard was set were where the wall was lowest and the enemy could more easily break it down or get over it, and that the enemies learnt their plan was known from the very preparations the Jews made to receive them.

Clarke draws a doctrine from the pairing of prayer and watch, that the strongest confidence in God's protection does not preclude the use of any means of self-preservation that his providence has put in our power, the power to will and the use of it being two distinct things. He calls the warning verse extremely difficult, points out that the words our translators supply have nothing correspondent in the Hebrew, prefers the Greek sense that they come up from all places against us, and proposes a one-letter emendation giving what they designed against us, for which three scholars contend although no manuscript supports it; he adds that the word counsel in the following verse countenances the change. On the appeal he asks whether the enemies are more terrible or stronger than God, itemises what was at stake in the brethren, sons, daughters, wives and houses the enemies meant to seize, and observes that a people fighting for religion, lives and property can never be conquered once they take up the sword. Wesley explains the complaint as coming from Jews partly terrified by their enemies and partly wearied with continual labour, with rubbish more than they could suddenly remove, takes the ten times as a certain number put for an uncertain, and glosses the posting as men set within the walls where these were not yet raised to their due height and on the tops of the finished walls and towers, whence they might shoot arrows or throw stones.

Henry marks three things in the conspiracy: it was unanimous, men of different interests made one by their opposition to the work of God; it was close, since they promised themselves success from the secrecy of it, saying the Jews shall not know, neither see; and it was cruel, since nothing less than the murder of the workmen would stop the work. He finds no quarrel behind it, no wrong done and none designed, but mere envy and malice, for they hated the Jews' piety and were vexed at their prosperity. On the discouragement he is blunt: can Judah, that warlike valiant tribe, sneak thus? Active leading men have as much ado to grapple with the fears of their friends as with the terrors of their enemies. He divides Nehemiah's response into looking up and looking about, since prayer without watchfulness is slothful and watchfulness without prayer is proud, and either way we forfeit God's protection. He credits the informers with honesty and affection enough to come themselves and say it ten times, and reads the abruptness of their message as the mark of men out of breath, whose looks made up the deficiency of their words. From the appeal he draws that the reigning fear of God is the best antidote against the ensnaring fear of man, and that setting the guards by families engaged mutual relations to mutual assistance.

debates: What the warning of the neighbouring Jews actually says, where Clarke calls the verse extremely difficult, notes that the supplied words have nothing in the Hebrew, prefers the Greek sense that they come up from all places against us, and proposes a one-letter emendation, while Ellicott reads it as repeated messages calling the builders home for their own protection.

What Nehemiah's looking means, where Gill takes it literally of a review of the people in their places and armed, Henry divides it into looking up to God and looking about him to set a watch, and Ellicott infers from it that the appeal was made on the actual approach of an attacking party.

Where the guards were posted, where Gill and Wesley take the lower places to be the unfinished stretches most open to assault, while Ellicott argues that the lower places were really the bare places, chosen because approaching foes could be seen from them at a distance.
outliers: Clarke adds that the word counsel in the notice of the plot's frustration countenances his conjectural emendation of the warning verse.
Wesley takes the ten times of the warning as a certain number put for an uncertain.

16.pericope_label: And it came to pass from that time forth, that the half of my servants wrought in the work, and the other half of them held both the spears, the shields, and the bows, and the habergeons; and the rulers were behind all the house of Judah. They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon. For the builders, every one had his sword girded by his side, and so builded. And he that sounded the trumpet was by me. And I said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, The work is great and large, and we are separated upon the wall, one far from another. In what place therefore ye hear the sound of the trumpet, resort ye thither unto us: our God shall fight for us. So we laboured in the work: and half of them held the spears from the rising of the morning till the stars appeared. Likewise at the same time said I unto the people, Let every one with his servant lodge within Jerusalem, that in the night they may be a guard to us, and labour on the day. So neither I, nor my brethren, nor my servants, nor the men of the guard which followed me, none of us put off our clothes, saving that every one put them off for washing.

schools.summary: Ellicott distinguishes Nehemiah's own servants from all the house of Judah, the former being divided into two parties, one working on what was unfinished and the other holding their weapons, and takes the note that the rulers were behind to mean they stood ready to lead the defence if necessary; habergeons he explains as coats of mail or corselets, thin plates of metal sewn upon leather. He divides the builders into masons, who built with both hands and kept their weapons at their side, and their burden-bearers, who held a weapon in one hand, and reads the notice that they laboured in the work as a general recapitulation with the added measure of the day's length during this pressing season. On the last clause he judges the rendering about washing very improbable, since the words are simply every man his weapon water, rejects the subtler turn that each man's weapon was his water, and prefers to supply the ellipsis, that every man went with his weapon to the water. Delitzsch identifies the servants as Nehemiah's personal retinue, placed at his disposal as governor for official purposes, gives Nehemiah's reason for the trumpet in his own words, that the work is great and wide and they are separated upon the wall one far from another, and insists that the order to lodge in Jerusalem was given to the labourers on the wall and not merely to the warriors of the community. He finds the closing words very obscure, admitting no tolerable sense whether the water is taken for drinking or for washing, and rejects an attempted emendation of them.

Clarke notes that the arrangement is no unusual thing even now in Palestine, where men sowing their seed are often attended by an armed man to prevent robbery, and that the image of one hand on the work and one on a weapon means a man had his arms at hand and was as ready to fight as to work, as a line of Ovid has one hand hold the pen and the other a drawn sword without meaning both at once. He sets out the danger the trumpet met, that with walls so extensive and the workmen so scattered the enemies might attack them successively, so Nehemiah ordered them to work as near each other as they could and kept a trumpeter always with him; and he explains the lodging order from custom, that the country people used to go home after the day's labour but were now obliged to sleep in Jerusalem, ready to help their brethren. On the obscure clause he assembles the ancient versions: the Latin has every one strip himself for the bath, the Greek omits the clause, the Syriac has none of us put off his clothes for a month each in his turn, and the Arabic that they did not put them off but with their arms at the end of a month. Wesley calls the one-hand image a proverbial speech, like saying of a man who pretends kindness that he carries bread in one hand and a stone in the other, and keeps the washing, referring it to cleansing from some impurity befalling them or their garments.

Henry notices that the builders returned to the wall without laying down their arms, since if one design failed the enemies would be hatching another, and guesses that the two parties changed services at stated hours, which would relieve the fatigue of both and ease the bearers of burdens whose strength had decayed. The image of working with one hand and holding a weapon with the other cannot be understood literally, he says, since the work would require both hands, but shows that they were equally employed in both. He observes that a sword at the side could be carried without hindering labour, and that the word of God is the sword of the Spirit, which we ought always to have at hand. On the trumpet he draws the distinction the whole arrangement rests on: as workmen they had to be dispersed wherever there was work to do, but as soldiers they had to come into close order and be found in a body, and so should the labourers in Christ's building be ready to unite against a common foe. He adds the maxim that the strength of a city lies more in its hands than in its walls, and presses the last detail, that the spears were held up from twilight to twilight and that while the heat of the business lasted neither Nehemiah nor his attendants went to bed but slept in their clothes, which was a sign their heart was upon their work.

debates: What the closing clause about clothes and water means, where Ellicott supplies an ellipsis and has every man go with his weapon to the water, Delitzsch declares the words obscure beyond any tolerable sense and rejects an emendation, Clarke lays out four ancient versions that disagree among themselves, and Wesley simply keeps the washing and refers it to ceremonial cleansing.

How literally the one hand on the work and one on a weapon should be taken, which Henry and Wesley both treat as proverbial rather than physical, Wesley comparing the man who carries bread in one hand and a stone in the other, while Ellicott divides the workers so that the burden-bearers really did hold a weapon in one hand.

Who was told to lodge within Jerusalem, where Delitzsch insists the order went to the labourers on the wall and not merely to the warriors of the community, while Clarke reads it as a change in the ordinary habit of country people going home after the day's labour.
outliers: Clarke observes that an armed escort for men at field work is no unusual thing even now in Palestine, where sowers are often attended by a guard against robbery.
Henry draws from the lodging order the maxim that the strength of a city lies more in its hands than in its walls.
